answers.answer: No second account is needed. Once Twitch is connected, the bot replies in chat right away. It uses the first connected account in this order: your own bot account (connected on White-label bot), then the shared bot of the installation, then your own Twitch account. With neither bot account connected, the lines come from your own Twitch account, so you can test a command such as !commands straight away.
answers.quote: You do not need to make a bot account first.

answers.answer: Twitch must be connected first, as the opening paragraph says, with a link to Connect platforms. To change the Bot line marker you must be the broadcaster, which is stated just above the marker steps. The shared bot is added only by the person who runs the installation, and the page says this in the shared bot paragraph.
answers.quote: After you connect Twitch, the bot can already reply in your chat.

answers.answer: Open Settings, then White-label bot in the Bot group, and read the one row in the card Your channel's own bot. A bot name with a Connected badge and an @ handle means your own bot account. The text Your channel uses the shared bot followed by a login name means the shared bot. Shared bot with nothing after it means your own Twitch account. For the marker, success is the message Basics saved. after Save, then !commands answered with the marker in front of the line.
answers.quote: Your own bot account is connected, and the bot types from it.

answers.answer: Because a separate bot account is connected, the bot types from that account and leaves the marker off. The marker can still be saved, but it never shows in chat, so nothing is broken. The moderator notice checks that same bot account. When it loses the moderator role, the notice BotName is not a moderator in your channel appears with that account's login name, in Needs attention and in the Action required list. The fix is to type /mod and the login name in your chat as the broadcaster and press Enter. The notice clears once Twitch reports the bot is a moderator again.
answers.quote: When either one is connected, the bot leaves the marker off.

answers.answer: In the first row of the order table, I would guess what 'is active' adds beyond 'connected'. The page never says how a connected bot account can be inactive or how to see that, though the Connected badge in the card seems to stand for it. The cost is a brief pause and one reread.
answers.quote: Your own bot account is connected on White-label bot and is active.

answers.answer: This sentence names the marker and the moderator notice before either one is explained, so a listener holds two unknown terms until later sections. The cost is small, because both are explained further down in reading order.
answers.quote: When it is connected, the bot types from it, leaves the marker off its lines, and the moderator notice checks this account.

warning_review.reason: Seventeen words over the diagnostic line costs this reader little. The first steps start near word 480, the answers to questions 1 and 2 sit in the opening paragraphs, and the answer to question 3 is in the short settings section, so no extra length stands between the reader and an action.

The 33-word sentence is the only definition of the Bot line marker and comes at the first place the reader meets the term, before the steps that set it. It is long to hear, but it carries one idea with a clear subject; splitting it would add a sentence without adding information.

The six sentences cover one edge case, the Sender field on a Send message step, and they come after the marker steps, not before them. A streamer who only needs the default can skip the paragraph, and the reader who needs the Broadcaster choice finds it in one place.

The paragraph gives the notice wording, where it appears and the fix, which is exactly what the application case needs: the reader sees the notice with the bot's login name and must type /mod. Its sentences follow the order of events, with nothing generic to cut.
